items.setupText: My driving lesson is from two to three.
items.taskText: What does 'lesson' mean here?
options: a time when you repair something
a journey you make to work
a time when someone teaches you
a break before you start work
items.answer: a time when someone teaches you
items.explanation: A lesson is a period of teaching, here learning to drive.

rationales.a time when someone teaches you: A lesson is a period of teaching, here learning to drive.
rationales.a time when you repair something: Repair work fixes something; a driving lesson teaches a skill.
rationales.a journey you make to work: A journey can involve driving, but 'lesson' names the teaching time.
rationales.a break before you start work: A lesson involves learning, not a rest from work.

findings: Bare start-time sentence and mixed word-class definitions did not test lesson in a useful context.
audit.microSkill: Lesson as a period of instruction
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes teaching outside a school classroom.
audit.levelReason: A familiar adult skill and short time phrase suit A1.
audit.similarityNote: Driving instruction, not class as a group or exam as assessment.

items.setupText: At the end of the language course, we have a short test.
items.taskText: What is the main purpose of the test?
options: to check what we have learned
to choose our next teacher
to buy our course books
to arrange our lesson times
items.answer: to check what we have learned
items.explanation: A course test checks learners' knowledge or skills.

rationales.to choose our next teacher: Choosing staff is not what 'test' means in this course.
rationales.to check what we have learned: A course test checks learners' knowledge or skills.
rationales.to buy our course books: Buying books is preparation, not a test of learning.
rationales.to arrange our lesson times: A timetable arranges times; a test checks learning.

findings: Unmotivated clinic setting blurred educational and medical senses; feedback only named other words.
audit.microSkill: Educational test purpose
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects test with checking learning rather than course administration.
audit.levelReason: Common course vocabulary with an explicit purpose question suits A1.
audit.similarityNote: Purpose of assessment, not interpreting a score.

items.setupText: Tutor: 'Where do you live?' Learner: 'In Lima.'
items.taskText: Which part is the learner's answer?
options: Tutor
Where do you live?
Learner
In Lima.
items.answer: In Lima.
items.explanation: An answer responds to a question; 'In Lima' gives the requested place.

rationales.Tutor: 'Tutor' names the person asking, not the reply.
rationales.Where do you live?: This asks for information; it is the question.
An answer responds to a question; 'In Lima' gives the requested place.
rationales.Learner: 'Learner' labels the speaker, not the words of the answer.

findings: Written-answer sentence lacked an actual question and mixed noun and verb glosses.
audit.microSkill: Recognizing an answer in a dialogue
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes speaker labels, question and response.
audit.levelReason: A familiar personal-information exchange is accessible at A1.
audit.similarityNote: Locating a reply, not selecting a collocation with answer.

items.setupText: After work, Mei studies English at home.
items.taskText: What does 'studies' mean here?
options: teaches other people
works to learn something
stops learning a subject
chooses a different language
items.answer: works to learn something
items.explanation: 'To study' is to spend time learning a subject, for example by reading and doing exercises.

rationales.teaches other people: Teaching helps others learn; this sentence describes Mei's own learning.
rationales.chooses a different language: Studying does not mean changing the subject she chose.
rationales.works to learn something: 'To study' is to spend time learning a subject, for example by reading and doing exercises.

findings: The example-says wrapper added nothing and the distractors differed in word class.
audit.microSkill: Study versus teach
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates learning a subject from helping others learn it.
audit.levelReason: Present simple and an adult evening routine suit A1.
audit.similarityNote: Learning activity, not the student role or practice noun.

items.setupText: Our talk is about food. Its title is 'A Taste of Home'.
items.taskText: What is the topic of the talk?
options: food
A Taste of Home
the person speaking
the room for the talk
items.answer: food
items.explanation: The topic is what a talk is about; here it is food.

rationales.food: The topic is what a talk is about; here it is food.
rationales.A Taste of Home: These words are the title, the name given to the talk.
rationales.the person speaking: The speaker gives the talk; 'topic' names its subject.
rationales.the room for the talk: The room is its location, not what it is about.

findings: Topic was matched against unrelated page and class meanings, with no title contrast.
audit.microSkill: Topic versus title
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes a subject from the name of a talk.
audit.levelReason: A short concrete subject and supplied title support A1.
audit.similarityNote: Content versus label, unlike B-level summary and main-point decisions.

items.setupText: Our English class has twelve adults from five countries.
items.taskText: What does 'class' mean in this sentence?
options: the room where we learn
the book we use to learn
the group learning together
the time when we have a break
items.answer: the group learning together
items.explanation: 'Class' can mean the learners taught together, as it does here.

rationales.the room where we learn: The room holds learners, but 'twelve adults' describes the group itself.
rationales.the group learning together: 'Class' can mean the learners taught together, as it does here.
rationales.the book we use to learn: A book contains material; it is not the group of adults.
rationales.the time when we have a break: The number and countries describe people, not a break time.

findings: Begins-at-ten frame repeated lesson and tested only the same event sense.
audit.microSkill: Class as a group of learners
audit.pedagogicalValue: Introduces a common group sense rather than assuming class always means a lesson.
audit.levelReason: Concrete people and numbers make the sense clear at A1.
audit.similarityNote: Group sense deliberately differs from item 1's teaching period.

items.setupText: The course book has printed lessons and exercises. I need a second book with empty pages for my own writing.
items.taskText: Which book do I need?
options: a dictionary
a textbook
a guidebook
a notebook
items.answer: a notebook
items.explanation: A notebook has space for your own writing, such as notes from class.

rationales.a dictionary: A dictionary gives word meanings; it is not a book of empty pages.
rationales.a textbook: The printed course book is a textbook; the second book is for your writing.
rationales.a notebook: A notebook has space for your own writing, such as notes from class.
rationales.a guidebook: A guidebook gives information about a place or activity rather than empty writing space.

findings: Book-on-table frame and pages-with-words definition were too broad to teach a useful distinction.
audit.microSkill: Notebook versus textbook
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes a writing resource from prepared learning material.
audit.levelReason: Physical books and their uses support an A1 choice.
audit.similarityNote: Learning materials, not borrowing from a library.

items.setupText: The tutor says, 'Turn to page six in your book.'
items.taskText: What should you look for?
options: the sixth book on the shelf
the side of a sheet numbered 6
the sixth word on the cover
the sixth lesson on the timetable
items.answer: the side of a sheet numbered 6
items.explanation: A page is one side of a sheet in a book; its printed number helps you find it.

rationales.the sixth book on the shelf: 'Page' refers to part of one book, not a separate book on a shelf.
rationales.the sixth word on the cover: A word is much smaller than the numbered page requested.
rationales.the sixth lesson on the timetable: The instruction names a page inside the book, not a lesson time.
rationales.the side of a sheet numbered 6: A page is one side of a sheet in a book; its printed number helps you find it.

findings: Open page five was awkward and the report wrapper was irrelevant.
audit.microSkill: Page reference in an instruction
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects a page number to the correct part of a printed book.
audit.levelReason: A simple classroom action and one number suit A1.
audit.similarityNote: Navigating a resource, not counting words.

items.setupText: On the board is the sentence 'I work here.'
items.taskText: Which choice is one whole word from the sentence?
options: work
w
work here
I work here.
items.answer: work
items.explanation: 'Work' is a complete word between the spaces in this sentence.

rationales.work: 'Work' is a complete word between the spaces in this sentence.
rationales.w: 'W' is one letter from 'work', not the whole word.
This is the whole three-word sentence, not one word.

findings: Abstract unit-of-language gloss and reception-desk tail obscured a basic distinction.
audit.microSkill: Word versus letter and sentence
audit.pedagogicalValue: Builds the vocabulary needed to follow language-learning instructions.
audit.levelReason: An actual three-word sentence makes the distinction visible at A1.
audit.similarityNote: Written-language units, not spelling a name on the phone.

items.setupText: Rosa helps the adults in our cooking course learn new skills. She plans the lessons.
items.taskText: What is Rosa's role in the course?
options: a visitor
the teacher
a customer
the receptionist
items.answer: the teacher
items.explanation: The teacher plans and leads learning, as Rosa does here.

rationales.a visitor: A visitor attends a place; the sentence gives Rosa responsibility for teaching.
rationales.the teacher: The teacher plans and leads learning, as Rosa does here.
rationales.a customer: A customer buys something; that is not the learning role described.
rationales.the receptionist: A receptionist welcomes people and handles enquiries, not necessarily their lessons.

findings: Person-who-teaches answer merely repeated the target word and unrelated noun foils were weak.
audit.microSkill: Teacher as the person leading learning
audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies a teaching role from concrete actions.
audit.levelReason: Familiar cooking skills and short sentences suit A1.
audit.similarityNote: Instructor's actions, contrasted with the adult learner in item 11.

items.setupText: Ben is 54. He works in a shop and goes to a college course on Fridays.
items.taskText: At college, Ben is a student. What does that mean?
options: He sells the course books.
He is learning on the course.
He teaches the Friday course.
He cleans the college rooms.
items.answer: He is learning on the course.
items.explanation: A student is someone studying; students can be adults of any age.

Selling books is a job; 'student' describes his learning role.
Teaching is the teacher's role; a student attends to learn.
A student is someone studying; students can be adults of any age.
Cleaning is not the meaning of 'student', even if a student also has a job.

findings: Student-has-book sentence offered little role evidence and mixed noun/verb definitions.
audit.microSkill: Student as an adult learning role
audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids treating student as a word restricted to children or full-time learners.
audit.levelReason: Age, work and a weekly course are concrete A1 information.
audit.similarityNote: Adult learner identity, not a second teacher definition.

items.setupText: The worksheet says, 'Match each word to a picture.'
items.taskText: What does 'match' ask you to do?
options: write each word three times
draw a new picture for each word
put each word with the right picture
read each word to the class
items.answer: put each word with the right picture
items.explanation: 'Match' means connect things that belong together, here words and their pictures.

rationales.write each word three times: Repeating the word practises writing; it does not connect words and pictures.
rationales.draw a new picture for each word: The instruction uses the pictures already provided.
rationales.read each word to the class: Reading aloud does not show which picture belongs with each word.
rationales.put each word with the right picture: 'Match' means connect things that belong together, here words and their pictures.

findings: Question-is-easy example repeated the answer/question distinction without supplying a question.
audit.microSkill: Match in a learning instruction
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches a frequent exercise command through the action it requires.
audit.levelReason: Concrete word-picture pairing is suitable foundational A1 vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Exercise command replaces another question definition.

items.setupText: The notice says, 'Final exam: Monday, 10 a.m. Bring a pen.'
items.taskText: What is happening on Monday?
options: the first lesson of the course
a test at the end of the course
a meeting to buy new pens
a break from the course
items.answer: a test at the end of the course
items.explanation: A final exam checks learning at the end of a course or stage.

rationales.a test at the end of the course: A final exam checks learning at the end of a course or stage.
rationales.the first lesson of the course: 'Final' points to the end; 'exam' names a test rather than a lesson.
rationales.a meeting to buy new pens: 'Bring a pen' tells you what to take, not the purpose of the event.
rationales.a break from the course: An exam is an assessment activity, not time away from learning.

findings: Exam-is-tomorrow frame repeated test with unrelated reading/listening foils.
audit.microSkill: Final exam in a course notice
audit.pedagogicalValue: Combines the event word with final and a practical instruction.
audit.levelReason: A brief notice with date, time and equipment suits A1.
audit.similarityNote: Understanding a notice, distinct from item 2's assessment purpose.

items.setupText: For this activity, read the message silently.
items.taskText: Which action follows that instruction?
options: Say the message so everyone hears it.
Listen while someone says the message.
Look at the written words without speaking.
Write the same message on a new page.
items.answer: Look at the written words without speaking.
items.explanation: 'Read silently' means take in the written message without saying it aloud.

'Silently' means without speaking; this would be reading aloud.
rationales.Look at the written words without speaki: 'Read silently' means take in the written message without saying it aloud.
Listening uses another person's voice; the instruction asks you to read.
Writing it again is copying, not the requested silent reading.

findings: Read definition was a generic word-list match with no distinction among plausible actions.
audit.microSkill: Read silently versus listen or copy
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates ways of working with the same message.
audit.levelReason: One simple adverb and familiar actions support A1.
audit.similarityNote: Silent reading, complementary to Collocations' read aloud rather than its duplicate.

items.setupText: The online exercise says, 'Write a short answer in the box.'
items.taskText: What should you put in the box?
options: words that answer the question
a recording of your voice
a picture of your face
a link to the next exercise
items.answer: words that answer the question
items.explanation: 'Write' asks you to produce written words, here by typing in the box.

rationales.a recording of your voice: A recording is a spoken answer; 'write' asks for written words.
rationales.a picture of your face: A photograph does not provide the requested written answer.
rationales.words that answer the question: 'Write' asks you to produce written words, here by typing in the box.
rationales.a link to the next exercise: The box is for your answer, not a way to move to another exercise.

findings: Write-your-name wrapper taught little beyond a generic definition and arbitrary foils.
audit.microSkill: Write as a required response mode
audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies written output in an online learning task.
audit.levelReason: Common online-course vocabulary and concrete choices suit A1.
audit.similarityNote: Producing a response, not reading or copying source text.

items.setupText: Close your books and listen to the recording.
items.taskText: What should you pay attention to?
options: the words on the next page
your partner's written answer
the pictures on the cover
the voices you can hear
items.answer: the voices you can hear
items.explanation: 'Listening' means paying attention to sound, here the recorded voices.

rationales.the words on the next page: The books are closed; this is not a reading task.
rationales.your partner's written answer: A written answer is something to read, not the recording named here.
rationales.the pictures on the cover: Pictures are visual; 'listen' directs attention to sound.
rationales.the voices you can hear: 'Listening' means paying attention to sound, here the recorded voices.

findings: In-the-office-email listen-to-the-teacher sentence was an unnatural frame.
audit.microSkill: Listen as attention to recorded speech
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects the learning command to sound rather than written material.
audit.levelReason: A short two-part instruction supports an A1 action choice.
audit.similarityNote: Understanding an audio-task command, not the preposition after listen.

items.setupText: The piano teacher says, 'Ten minutes of practice every day will help.'
items.taskText: What does 'practice' mean here?
options: time spent choosing an instrument
time spent watching a concert
time spent waiting for a lesson
time spent playing to improve
items.answer: time spent playing to improve
items.explanation: Practice is activity done to develop a skill, here playing the piano regularly.

rationales.time spent playing to improve: Practice is activity done to develop a skill, here playing the piano regularly.
rationales.time spent choosing an instrument: Choosing is preparation; it is not working on the playing skill.
rationales.time spent watching a concert: Watching may be useful, but 'practice' here means doing the playing yourself.
rationales.time spent waiting for a lesson: Waiting does not involve the repeated work the teacher recommends.

findings: Practice was a noun but its keyed gloss repeat to improve was a verb phrase.
audit.microSkill: Practice as skill-building activity
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains the noun through what a learner does, with matching noun-phrase options.
audit.levelReason: A familiar hobby and daily time amount suit A1.
audit.similarityNote: Regular skill work, not the more general study-English activity.

items.setupText: The quiz gives one point for each correct answer. My score is 8 out of 10.
items.taskText: What does my score tell me?
options: how many minutes I used
how many pages I read
how many quizzes I took
how many points I got
items.answer: how many points I got
items.explanation: Your score is the points awarded: eight from a possible ten.

rationales.how many minutes I used: A score measures points here, not time.
rationales.how many points I got: Your score is the points awarded: eight from a possible ten.
rationales.how many pages I read: Page count is not what the quiz awards points for.
rationales.how many quizzes I took: 'Eight out of ten' is the result of this quiz, not a count of quizzes.

findings: High score at the start of an activity had no basis and unrelated glossary foils.
audit.microSkill: Quiz score as awarded points
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects score to a concrete result rather than completion time.
audit.levelReason: Small numbers and an explicit scoring rule suit A1.
audit.similarityNote: Reading an outcome, not defining the exam event.

items.setupText: I borrow course books from the college library and bring them back two weeks later.
items.taskText: Which description fits this library?
options: a shop where I buy my lunch
an office where I pay my course fee
a place where I can borrow books
a room where I sell my old books
items.answer: a place where I can borrow books
items.explanation: A library provides books and other resources for people to use or borrow.

rationales.a shop where I buy my lunch: Lunch is bought at a food shop or cafe, not borrowed as course books.
rationales.an office where I pay my course fee: The sentence describes borrowing books, not paying for the course.
rationales.a place where I can borrow books: A library provides books and other resources for people to use or borrow.
rationales.a room where I sell my old books: These books must be returned; selling books is a different activity.

findings: Place-with-books was broad enough to include a bookshop and the closing-time tail added no distinction.
audit.microSkill: Library borrowing versus buying books
audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies a learning resource through borrowing and returning.
audit.levelReason: An everyday adult-college action suits A1.
audit.similarityNote: Access to resources, not the notebook/textbook distinction.

items.setupText: After the evening lesson, our tutor gives us two exercises to finish before the next class.
items.taskText: What is this homework?
options: course work to do outside the lesson
cleaning the rooms in our homes
work we do for our employers
a lesson taught in our homes
items.answer: course work to do outside the lesson
items.explanation: Homework is work set for learners to complete outside class; it can be done in a library too.

rationales.cleaning the rooms in our homes: Cleaning is housework, not work set by a tutor.
rationales.work we do for our employers: Paid job tasks are work, but not homework set on this course.
rationales.a lesson taught in our homes: 'Homework' is a learner's task, not necessarily a lesson or something done at home.
rationales.course work to do outside the lesson: Homework is work set for learners to complete outside class; it can be done in a library too.

findings: Homework-is-short sentence lacked a useful contrast with housework or employment.
audit.microSkill: Homework versus housework
audit.pedagogicalValue: Clarifies that homework is defined by the learning task, not simply its location.
audit.levelReason: Two simple exercises after an evening course suit A1.
audit.similarityNote: Task category, not Collocations' do homework verb choice.

items.setupText: One learner remembers new words with pictures. Another uses short recordings.
items.taskText: They use different methods. What does 'methods' mean here?
options: reasons for joining
subjects to learn
results of learning
ways of learning
items.answer: ways of learning
items.explanation: A method is a way of doing something; pictures and recordings are different ways to learn words.

rationales.ways of learning: A method is a way of doing something; pictures and recordings are different ways to learn words.
rationales.reasons for joining: A reason explains why they joined, not how they learn.
rationales.subjects to learn: Both learners are working on words; 'method' describes their approach, not a different subject.
rationales.results of learning: Results come from the activity; the methods are ways of doing it.

findings: A new method was named without showing a method; feedback was dictionary cross-matching.
audit.microSkill: Method as how learning is done
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates a way of working from its purpose, subject and result.
audit.levelReason: Two concrete learning activities support an introductory A2 use.
audit.similarityNote: Learning approach, not a technical research methodology.

items.setupText: For my local-history project, I found the year the bridge opened in a newspaper article.
items.taskText: The tutor asks for my source. What should I name?
options: the title of my project
the day I finished writing
the newspaper article
the place where I sat to read
items.answer: the newspaper article
items.explanation: A source is where information comes from, here the article you read.

rationales.the title of my project: Your project uses the information; it is not where you found it.
rationales.the newspaper article: A source is where information comes from, here the article you read.
rationales.the day I finished writing: That is your work date, not the source of the bridge information.
rationales.the place where I sat to read: Your reading location does not identify the material containing the information.

findings: Include the source supplied no actual information source to distinguish from other report details.
audit.microSkill: Source as the origin of information
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects source to the material used, not the learner's product or location.
audit.levelReason: One fact from one named article makes this academic foundation accessible at A2.
audit.similarityNote: Basic source identification, before advanced citation and provenance distinctions.

items.setupText: A course page gives two statements: 'The building opened in 1998' and 'It is the nicest building in town.'
items.taskText: Which word describes the second statement as a personal view?
options: a date
an opinion
a measurement
an instruction
items.answer: an opinion
items.explanation: An opinion is a person's view; 'nicest' depends on what someone likes.

rationales.a date: A date tells when something happened; 'nicest' expresses a judgment.
rationales.a measurement: A measurement gives an amount or size, not a personal judgment of beauty.
rationales.an opinion: An opinion is a person's view; 'nicest' depends on what someone likes.
rationales.an instruction: An instruction tells someone what to do; this statement expresses a view.

findings: The chart-gives-evidence sentence contained no chart or supported claim and was abstract for A2.
audit.microSkill: Opinion as a personal evaluation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes an evaluative view from dates, measurements and commands.
audit.levelReason: A familiar building and a basic superlative support A2 interpretation.
audit.similarityNote: Opinion foundation replaces unsupported evidence terminology.

items.setupText: During a talk, Sam writes 'bus: cheaper; train: faster' to help him remember.
items.taskText: What are these notes?
options: short pieces of written information
the exact words of the whole talk
questions sent to the speaker
marks showing his test result
items.answer: short pieces of written information
items.explanation: Notes record useful information briefly, often without full sentences.

rationales.the exact words of the whole talk: Notes can be short reminders; Sam has not written the complete talk.
rationales.questions sent to the speaker: These phrases record information rather than ask the speaker anything.
rationales.marks showing his test result: There is no assessment here; the writing helps Sam remember.
rationales.short pieces of written information: Notes record useful information briefly, often without full sentences.

findings: Cost is one factor was context-free and used abstract result definitions for a beginner band.
audit.microSkill: Notes as brief learning records
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes useful shortened writing without treating it as a full transcript.
audit.levelReason: Two everyday travel comparisons keep the reading demand at A2.
audit.similarityNote: Personal note-taking, not verb collocations about writing.

items.setupText: The course aim is to help adults use email. At the start, many learners cannot send a message.
items.taskText: What does 'aim' mean here?
options: what learners have already achieved
how long each lesson lasts
what the course wants to achieve
how much the course costs
items.answer: what the course wants to achieve
items.explanation: An aim is an intended result, even before learners have reached it.

rationales.what the course wants to achieve: An aim is an intended result, even before learners have reached it.
rationales.what learners have already achieved: That would be an actual result; an aim says what is intended.
rationales.how long each lesson lasts: Lesson length is a time detail, not the learning aim.
rationales.how much the course costs: The fee is a cost, not what the course hopes learners can do.

findings: Positive outcome duplicated the later result item with no event explaining either.
audit.microSkill: Aim versus achieved result
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes an intended learning goal from an accomplishment.
audit.levelReason: A familiar email skill supports A2 purpose vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Intended result contrasted with item 31's actual result.

items.setupText: A dictionary entry says: 'island: land with water all around it'.
items.taskText: Which part is the definition?
options: island
land with water all around it
the name of the dictionary
the page number of the entry
items.answer: land with water all around it
items.explanation: A definition explains what a word means; these words explain 'island'.

rationales.island: 'Island' is the word being explained, not its explanation.
rationales.land with water all around it: A definition explains what a word means; these words explain 'island'.
rationales.the name of the dictionary: The dictionary's name identifies the book, not the meaning of 'island'.
rationales.the page number of the entry: A page number helps locate the entry but does not explain the word.

findings: Dictionary-gives-definition sentence named the object but provided no definition to recognize.
audit.microSkill: Definition versus headword and reference details
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches learners to locate the meaning within a dictionary entry.
audit.levelReason: A concrete familiar noun makes the reading task manageable at A2.
audit.similarityNote: Identifying an explanation, not the example in item 27.

items.setupText: The tutor says, 'Some courses teach practical skills. For example, this college offers bicycle repair.'
items.taskText: What is the example doing?
options: naming every course at the college
explaining why the college opened
telling learners to repair their bikes
giving one case of a practical course
items.answer: giving one case of a practical course
items.explanation: An example is a particular case used to make a general idea clearer.

rationales.naming every course at the college: One course is named; the tutor has not provided the full list.
rationales.explaining why the college opened: The sentence says nothing about the reason the college began.
rationales.giving one case of a practical course: An example is a particular case used to make a general idea clearer.
rationales.telling learners to repair their bikes: Mentioning a course is not an instruction to do the repair now.

findings: Teacher gave an example contained no example and used unrelated glossary foils.
audit.microSkill: Example as one case illustrating an idea
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes illustration from a complete list or instruction.
audit.levelReason: A concrete adult course illustrates a simple general category at A2.
audit.similarityNote: Particular case, distinct from a dictionary definition.

items.setupText: Your report has three separate blocks of writing. Each begins on a new line and develops one point.
items.taskText: What do we call these blocks of writing?
options: paragraphs
headings
letters
titles
items.answer: paragraphs
items.explanation: Paragraphs organize writing into separate units, usually developing a point in one or more sentences.

rationales.headings: Headings name sections; these blocks develop points in the report.
rationales.letters: Letters are individual written symbols, not blocks developing ideas.
rationales.titles: Titles name a whole work or section rather than give the developed explanation.
rationales.paragraphs: Paragraphs organize writing into separate units, usually developing a point in one or more sentences.

findings: A group of sentences was too loose a definition and implied every paragraph must have several sentences.
audit.microSkill: Paragraph as an organized unit of writing
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects paragraph with layout and development without imposing a fixed sentence count.
audit.levelReason: Concrete text layout supports A2 study vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Writing organization, not A1's single-word identification.

items.setupText: On this course, written work receives A, B, C or D. My essay received a grade of B.
items.taskText: What does 'grade' mean here?
options: a rating of my work
my current year level at school
the number of words I wrote
a comment about one spelling error
items.answer: a rating of my work
items.explanation: A grade shows how work was assessed; this course uses letters for its ratings.

rationales.a rating of my work: A grade shows how work was assessed; this course uses letters for its ratings.
rationales.my current year level at school: 'Grade' can refer to a school year in some varieties, but here it rates an essay.
rationales.the number of words I wrote: 'B' is the assessment result, not a word count.
rationales.a comment about one spelling error: A grade is the overall rating here; a detailed comment explains a specific issue.

findings: Reception-desk setting did not distinguish assessment grade from other established senses.
audit.microSkill: Grade as a rating rather than a school year
audit.pedagogicalValue: Uses explicit context to select a common educational sense without rejecting another variety.
audit.levelReason: A supplied letter scale avoids specialist grading knowledge at A2.
audit.similarityNote: Qualitative rating, not A1's numerical quiz score.

items.setupText: Marta is choosing between history and computing at college.
items.taskText: These are subjects. What does 'subjects' mean here?
options: people taking part in a study
pieces of work she must hand in
rooms where lessons take place
areas she can study
items.answer: areas she can study
items.explanation: A subject is an area of knowledge studied on a course, such as history.

rationales.people taking part in a study: 'Subjects' can mean participants, but history and computing are not people.
rationales.areas she can study: A subject is an area of knowledge studied on a course, such as history.
rationales.pieces of work she must hand in: Assignments are pieces of work; subjects are the areas the work concerns.
rationales.rooms where lessons take place: Subjects name what is studied, not the location of teaching.

findings: Favorite-subject frame gave only unrelated definitions and no other educational senses.
audit.microSkill: Subject as an area of study
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates the discipline from participants, tasks and rooms.
audit.levelReason: Choosing between two familiar courses suits A2.
audit.similarityNote: Course area, not A1's topic/title relation within one talk.

items.setupText: Learners tested two paper designs. The result was that the folded design held more weight.
items.taskText: Which question does the result answer?
options: What materials will we need?
What do we hope will happen?
What happened in the test?
Who suggested doing the test?
items.answer: What happened in the test?
items.explanation: A result is what an activity or test produced, here the difference in weight held.

rationales.What materials will we need?: That asks about preparation before the test, not its outcome.
rationales.What do we hope will happen?: A hope is an aim or prediction; a result reports what actually happened.
rationales.What happened in the test?: A result is what an activity or test produced, here the difference in weight held.
rationales.Who suggested doing the test?: The originator's identity does not tell us the outcome.

findings: Surprising result supplied no event and duplicated the equally bare outcome item.
audit.microSkill: Result as an observed outcome
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates what happened from preparation, intention and authorship.
audit.levelReason: A simple physical comparison supports A2 academic vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Actual outcome, not item 25's course aim.

items.setupText: For a project on local shops, we read old records and ask long-time residents questions. Our research takes a month.
items.taskText: What does 'research' name here?
options: the final talk we give
the work we do to find information
the pictures on our front page
the marks our tutor gives
items.answer: the work we do to find information
items.explanation: Research involves investigating a subject to learn more about it, using sources such as records and interviews.

rationales.the final talk we give: A talk may report the research; 'research' names the investigation itself.
rationales.the pictures on our front page: Pictures can be part of a project but are not the whole investigation.
rationales.the marks our tutor gives: Marks assess the work; they are not the work of finding things out.
rationales.the work we do to find information: Research involves investigating a subject to learn more about it, using sources such as records and interviews.

findings: Simple research gave no activity, while the survey foil could be part of research.
audit.microSkill: Research as investigation rather than its presentation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects the general word to several concrete information-gathering activities.
audit.levelReason: A local project provides accessible foundations for A2 learners.
audit.similarityNote: Investigation as a whole, not identifying a single source.

items.setupText: The college sends learners six questions about their journey to class. It collects the answers in a survey.
items.taskText: Why is this a survey rather than a test of their English?
options: It gives a mark for each travel choice.
It teaches learners a new bus route.
It checks whether learners know the timetable.
It collects information about learners' journeys.
items.answer: It collects information about learners' journeys.
items.explanation: A survey gathers information or views; these questions ask about people's travel experiences.

rationales.It collects information about learners': A survey gathers information or views; these questions ask about people's travel experiences.
The journeys are information to collect, not right or wrong answers to score.
A survey asks for information; it is not a lesson explaining a route.
rationales.It checks whether learners know the time: The questions concern their journeys, not knowledge of correct timetable answers.

findings: Ten-question survey could look like a test; generic feedback never distinguished purposes.
audit.microSkill: Survey versus knowledge test
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes gathering people's information from marking correct answers.
audit.levelReason: Routine journeys and a short questionnaire suit A2.
audit.similarityNote: Data-collection purpose, not the broader research activity.

items.setupText: The report shows each course's learner numbers with bars of different lengths.
items.taskText: What is this way of showing information called?
options: a chart
a timetable
a dictionary
a questionnaire
items.answer: a chart
items.explanation: A chart presents information visually; bars can show and compare amounts.

rationales.a timetable: A timetable arranges events by time; these bars compare numbers of learners.
rationales.a chart: A chart presents information visually; bars can show and compare amounts.
rationales.a dictionary: A dictionary explains words rather than compares course numbers with bars.
rationales.a questionnaire: A questionnaire asks questions; this display shows information already collected.

findings: Picture showing information was vague and mixed chart nouns with compare and summarize verb glosses.
audit.microSkill: Chart as a visual display of amounts
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes a display of collected information from a collection tool.
audit.levelReason: Bars of different lengths are a concrete A2 description without requiring a graphic.
audit.similarityNote: Information display, not numerical calculation.

items.setupText: Four learners came in the morning and six in the afternoon. The total was ten.
items.taskText: What does 'total' mean here?
options: the largest of the two groups
the number from both groups together
the number in each group
the difference between the groups
items.answer: the number from both groups together
items.explanation: A total is the whole amount after the parts are added together.

rationales.the largest of the two groups: The larger group has six; 'total' combines both groups.
rationales.the number in each group: The groups have different numbers, four and six; ten is not the count in each.
rationales.the number from both groups together: A total is the whole amount after the parts are added together.
rationales.the difference between the groups: The difference is two; 'total' refers to combining, not subtracting.

findings: Typical middle amount blurred different average measures and gave no numerical basis.
audit.microSkill: Total versus difference or largest amount
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches a clear quantity word without a misleading definition of average.
audit.levelReason: Small supplied numbers support an A2 vocabulary decision rather than difficult arithmetic.
audit.similarityNote: Combined amount replaces imprecise statistical terminology.

items.setupText: The task says, 'Compare the two college websites.'
items.taskText: Which action matches 'compare'?
options: Copy the words from one website.
Choose a website without looking at the other.
Find ways the websites are alike or different.
Write instructions for building a website.
items.answer: Find ways the websites are alike or different.
items.explanation: 'Compare' means examine things in relation to each other, including similarities and differences.

Copying reproduces text; it does not examine the two sites together.
rationales.Choose a website without looking at the: Comparison requires considering both, not choosing after viewing only one.
rationales.Write instructions for building a websit: That describes a procedure, not similarities or differences between these sites.
rationales.Find ways the websites are alike or diff: 'Compare' means examine things in relation to each other, including similarities and differences.

findings: Office-email wrapper was irrelevant and noun glosses made the verb answer conspicuous.
audit.microSkill: Compare as examining similarities and differences
audit.pedagogicalValue: Translates a common study command into the required activity.
audit.levelReason: Two familiar websites provide an accessible A2 comparison task.
audit.similarityNote: Relational study action, not selecting which source is better.

items.setupText: The tutor asks for a summary of a long talk in three sentences.
items.taskText: What should the summary contain?
options: the main points in a short form
the exact words of the whole talk
only your opinion of the speaker
new information on another topic
items.answer: the main points in a short form
items.explanation: A summary gives the important points briefly, leaving out many details.

rationales.the main points in a short form: A summary gives the important points briefly, leaving out many details.
rationales.the exact words of the whole talk: A complete record is not a short summary.
rationales.only your opinion of the speaker: An opinion evaluates the speaker; a summary reports the talk's main content.
rationales.new information on another topic: A summary stays with the original material rather than introduces an unrelated topic.

findings: Summarize-article request used unrelated noun meanings and no constraints on the product.
audit.microSkill: Summary as brief main content
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes summarizing from transcription and personal evaluation.
audit.levelReason: A clear three-sentence limit supports the introductory A2 meaning.
audit.similarityNote: Condensed account, not short notes made while listening.

items.setupText: A worksheet asks you to identify the capital city named in a short text.
items.taskText: What does 'identify' ask you to do?
options: explain the city's whole history
replace it with a different city
find it and say which city it is
decide whether you like the city
items.answer: find it and say which city it is
items.explanation: 'Identify' means recognize or name the thing requested.

rationales.explain the city's whole history: 'Identify' asks which city it is, not for a full historical explanation.
rationales.find it and say which city it is: 'Identify' means recognize or name the thing requested.
rationales.replace it with a different city: Changing the city is editing the information, not identifying it.
rationales.decide whether you like the city: Personal preference does not identify the city mentioned.

findings: Identify the main idea added an interpretive demand without a text and offered mixed word classes.
audit.microSkill: Identify as recognizing and naming
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates naming a requested item from explaining, editing or evaluating it.
audit.levelReason: A single concrete city is a manageable A2 referent.
audit.similarityNote: Finding a named item, not deriving an implied main idea.

items.setupText: The lesson moved online because the college building had no heating.
items.taskText: Which words give the reason for the change?
options: The lesson
the college building had no heating
moved online
the college building
items.answer: the college building had no heating
items.explanation: A reason explains why something happened; the heating problem explains the move.

rationales.The lesson: These words name the event, not why its location changed.
rationales.moved online: This describes the change itself, not the reason for it.
rationales.the college building had no heating: A reason explains why something happened; the heating problem explains the move.
rationales.the college building: Naming the building alone does not explain the problem that caused the change.

findings: Unclear reason supplied no actual cause and only dictionary matching.
audit.microSkill: Reason versus the event it explains
audit.pedagogicalValue: Locates the explanation of a change in a complete sentence.
audit.levelReason: A familiar disruption and because clause support A2.
audit.similarityNote: Cause of a course change, not a learner's intended aim.

items.setupText: The article is about a new public garden. It says the gates open at seven each morning.
items.taskText: The opening time is a detail. What does 'detail' mean here?
options: the whole subject of the article
the name given to the article
a reason the article was written
one specific piece of information
items.answer: one specific piece of information
items.explanation: A detail is a particular part of a larger account, such as an exact opening time.

rationales.the whole subject of the article: The subject is the garden; the time is one specific part of the information.
rationales.the name given to the article: A title names the article, not a particular opening-time fact.
rationales.a reason the article was written: The opening time does not explain the writer's purpose.
rationales.one specific piece of information: A detail is a particular part of a larger account, such as an exact opening time.

findings: Use one detail could also ask for evidence, so the original foil was not cleanly distinct.
audit.microSkill: Detail as specific information within a larger account
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes a particular fact from the subject, title and purpose.
audit.levelReason: A familiar garden and one time fact suit A2.
audit.similarityNote: Specific detail closes the foundation set without repeating source or summary.

items.setupText: On a map in the geography textbook, blue lines indicate rivers.
items.taskText: What do the blue lines do?
options: cause rivers to change direction
measure how deep rivers are
explain why rivers formed
show where rivers are
items.answer: show where rivers are
items.explanation: 'Indicate' can mean show or point out; the lines represent the rivers' locations.

rationales.cause rivers to change direction: 'Indicate' describes representation on the map, not an effect on real rivers.
rationales.show where rivers are: 'Indicate' can mean show or point out; the lines represent the rivers' locations.
rationales.measure how deep rivers are: The sentence assigns the lines a location function, not a depth scale.
rationales.explain why rivers formed: A symbol can show a river without explaining its origin.

findings: Exit-arrow item mixed adjectives, nouns and verbs in its alternatives and had weak academic fit.
audit.microSkill: Indicate as represent in a diagram
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes showing a feature from causing, measuring or explaining it.
audit.levelReason: An academic map context extends a familiar verb at B1.
audit.similarityNote: Visual indication, not evidential uncertainty or trend interpretation.

items.setupText: A historian calls the opening of the first public school a significant event in the town's history.
items.taskText: The history book is not reporting a statistical test. What does 'significant' mean here?
options: difficult to date precisely
mentioned only in private records
recent compared with other events
important in the town's development
items.answer: important in the town's development
items.explanation: 'Significant' in this ordinary historical use means important or meaningful.

rationales.difficult to date precisely: An event's significance does not tell us whether its date is known.
rationales.mentioned only in private records: The adjective does not specify where records are kept.
rationales.important in the town's development: 'Significant' in this ordinary historical use means important or meaningful.
rationales.recent compared with other events: An event can be significant whether it happened recently or long ago.

findings: Clinic context left ordinary importance and statistical significance unresolved.
audit.microSkill: Significant in its ordinary importance sense
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates importance from recency, uncertainty and technical statistical use.
audit.levelReason: A historical event provides a B1 abstract adjective in a clear sense.
audit.similarityNote: Importance explicitly distinguished from the advanced technical use.

items.setupText: Before asking the learners, the tutor plans an online task on the assumption that everyone has home internet.
items.taskText: What is the assumption?
options: a question learners have answered
an idea taken as true without checking
a result established by the task
a rule learners must follow
items.answer: an idea taken as true without checking
items.explanation: An assumption is something accepted as a starting point; here internet access has not been checked.

rationales.a question learners have answered: The tutor has not yet asked them, so this is not a collected answer.
rationales.a result established by the task: The task is still being planned; it has not produced this result.
rationales.a rule learners must follow: Having internet is being taken as true, not imposed as a rule.
rationales.an idea taken as true without checking: An assumption is something accepted as a starting point; here internet access has not been checked.

findings: Plan-based-on-assumption example did not reveal what was assumed or whether it had been checked.
audit.microSkill: Assumption as an unverified starting point
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows that an assumption need not be a known fact or necessarily false.
audit.levelReason: A practical course plan and an explicit before relationship suit B1.
audit.similarityNote: Recognizing a premise, not Collocations' act of challenging it.

items.setupText: The group has collected a month's bus arrival times. It will now analyze the data.
items.taskText: Which activity is analysis rather than collection or presentation alone?
options: Recording another month's arrival times
Copying the unchanged list onto a slide
Examining the times to find patterns in delays
Saving the list in a new folder
items.answer: Examining the times to find patterns in delays
items.explanation: Analysis examines information and relationships to understand what the data show.

rationales.Examining the times to find patterns in: Analysis examines information and relationships to understand what the data show.
rationales.Recording another month's arrival times: That gathers more data; it does not by itself analyze what has been collected.
rationales.Copying the unchanged list onto a slide: Copying changes the display, but does not itself examine patterns.
rationales.Saving the list in a new folder: Saving stores the data rather than studies their meaning or relationships.

findings: Study carefully gloss lacked a concrete analytical operation and used nonverb foils.
audit.microSkill: Analyze versus collect, copy and store data
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects analysis with examining patterns rather than any handling of information.
audit.levelReason: Familiar bus delays make a study process accessible at B1.
audit.similarityNote: Data examination, not the later interpret-a-graph meaning task.

items.setupText: You are explaining why adults choose evening courses. A tutor asks for relevant details.
items.taskText: Which detail is directly relevant to that question?
options: The college changed its logo last year.
The oldest classroom has green walls.
Many learners work during the day.
The library has books on local history.
items.answer: Many learners work during the day.
items.explanation: Relevant information connects to the question; daytime work helps explain choosing evening study.

A logo change does not explain learners' choice of lesson time.
Relevant information connects to the question; daytime work helps explain choosing evening study.
Wall color does not directly explain why adults choose evening classes.
The library's subject collection does not address the timing choice.

findings: Door-sign instruction had no topic against which relevance could be judged.
audit.microSkill: Relevant information relative to a stated question
audit.pedagogicalValue: Makes relevance depend on the inquiry rather than whether a fact is interesting.
audit.levelReason: An everyday time-choice explanation supports B1 reasoning.
audit.similarityNote: Question-directed relevance, not generic irrelevant-conversation idioms.

items.setupText: A report claims that its new reading app improves concentration, but gives no supporting results.
items.taskText: What does 'claims' tell us about that statement?
options: The report asks whether the app helps.
The report has withdrawn the statement.
The report presents the statement as true.
The report proves the statement is false.
items.answer: The report presents the statement as true.
items.explanation: 'To claim' is to assert that something is true; the word does not itself establish proof.

A claim asserts something; it is not just a question.
'Claims' presents the statement rather than takes it back.
rationales.The report presents the statement as tru: 'To claim' is to assert that something is true; the word does not itself establish proof.
rationales.The report proves the statement is false: The absence of support does not prove falsehood, and 'claim' does not mean 'disprove'.

findings: Claim-needs-evidence frame gave no actual assertion and only a dictionary definition.
audit.microSkill: Claim as assertion rather than proof
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates what a source asserts from whether the assertion is supported.
audit.levelReason: A familiar app and a simple contrast between assertion and results suit B1.
audit.similarityNote: Statement status, not advanced attribution or editorial tone.

items.setupText: For a pronunciation study, researchers collected audio recordings and written comments from learners.
items.taskText: Which description of these data is accurate?
options: Only the numbers of recordings count as data.
The recordings and comments are information for analysis.
The researchers' future predictions are the collected data.
The instructions to the participants are the results.
items.answer: The recordings and comments are information for analysis.
items.explanation: Data are information collected for use or analysis and can take spoken, written or numerical forms.

rationales.Only the numbers of recordings count as: Data can include recordings and words, not only numbers.
rationales.The researchers' future predictions are: Predictions are expectations; the recordings and comments are what was actually collected.
rationales.The instructions to the participants are: Instructions organize the activity; they are not the collected responses described.
rationales.The recordings and comments are informat: Data are information collected for use or analysis and can take spoken, written or numerical forms.

findings: Data-from-survey frame did not distinguish data from conclusions or avoid a numbers-only misconception.
audit.microSkill: Data beyond numerical measurements
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes qualitative material as data without testing disputed singular/plural usage.
audit.levelReason: Familiar recordings and comments support B1 study vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Forms of collected information, not analysis as an action.

items.setupText: A report has sections called 'Background', 'Method' and 'Results'. Each contains several paragraphs.
items.taskText: What is a section in this report?
options: a larger part devoted to one aspect
one sentence ending with a full stop
the complete report with its cover
a list of spelling corrections
items.answer: a larger part devoted to one aspect
items.explanation: A section organizes a report into a major part, which may contain several paragraphs.

rationales.a larger part devoted to one aspect: A section organizes a report into a major part, which may contain several paragraphs.
rationales.one sentence ending with a full stop: A sentence is a smaller grammatical unit, not the named report division.
rationales.the complete report with its cover: A section is part of the report, not the whole document.
rationales.a list of spelling corrections: Corrections may concern a section, but do not define its organizational role.

findings: Short final section supplied no document structure and three foils were verbs.
audit.microSkill: Section within a report hierarchy
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes major divisions from paragraphs and sentences.
audit.levelReason: Named report sections extend A2 paragraph knowledge at B1.
audit.similarityNote: Document hierarchy, not rearranging an essay's argument.

items.setupText: A graph shows weekly participation as 40, 42, 55 and 58. Weekend sessions began after the second week. The tutor asks learners to interpret the graph.
items.taskText: Which response interprets the pattern rather than simply describes the display?
options: The first bar is labeled 40.
Participation rose after weekend sessions were added.
There are four bars on the page.
The graph has a label for each week.
items.answer: Participation rose after weekend sessions were added.
items.explanation: Interpretation explains what the information shows; this describes a pattern without claiming the timing proves a cause.

This reads one value but does not explain what the pattern means.
rationales.Participation rose after weekend session: Interpretation explains what the information shows; this describes a pattern without claiming the timing proves a cause.
Counting bars describes the display, not the meaning of its data.
Labels organize the display; naming them does not interpret the participation pattern.

findings: Explain the meaning and state the meaning overlapped; reception-desk setting was irrelevant.
audit.microSkill: Interpret information versus describe its display
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes meaningful pattern description from isolated values and visual features.
audit.levelReason: A straightforward time pattern supports B1 interpretation vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Meaning of a display, not a literary reading attributed to a reviewer.

items.setupText: After comparing the two versions, the tutor concludes that the shorter instructions are easier to follow.
items.taskText: What does 'concludes' mean in this sentence?
options: starts the comparison with a question
finishes the lesson without giving a view
reaches a judgment from the comparison
defines the word 'instructions'
items.answer: reaches a judgment from the comparison
items.explanation: 'Conclude that' means reach a view after considering information or reasons.

rationales.starts the comparison with a question: The comparison precedes the judgment; 'concludes' names the resulting view.
rationales.finishes the lesson without giving a vie: 'Conclude' can mean 'finish', but 'concludes that' introduces a judgment here.
rationales.reaches a judgment from the comparison: 'Conclude that' means reach a view after considering information or reasons.
rationales.defines the word 'instructions': A definition explains a word; this statement judges the two versions.

findings: Decide after thinking was loose and the original did not distinguish inferential conclude from finish.
audit.microSkill: Conclude that versus conclude an event
audit.pedagogicalValue: Uses the following that clause to recognize a reasoned judgment.
audit.levelReason: A familiar comparison and a common reporting pattern suit B1.
audit.similarityNote: Reasoned conclusion sense, distinct from report-section naming.

items.setupText: The guide says, "In this chapter, the term 'habitat' means the natural place where a living thing lives."
items.taskText: What does 'term' mean here?
options: a period in the teaching year
a word used for a particular idea
a rule agreed in a contract
the final date for an assignment
items.answer: a word used for a particular idea
items.explanation: A term is a word or expression with a particular meaning in a subject.

rationales.a period in the teaching year: 'Term' can name a teaching period, but here it labels 'habitat' as vocabulary.
rationales.a rule agreed in a contract: 'Terms' can be conditions, but this sentence is explaining a word.
rationales.the final date for an assignment: The sentence gives no deadline; it defines 'habitat'.
rationales.a word used for a particular idea: A term is a word or expression with a particular meaning in a subject.

findings: Define repeated A2 definition with no new demand and unrelated process/structure foils.
audit.microSkill: Term as subject vocabulary
audit.pedagogicalValue: Selects the academic vocabulary sense among established meanings of term.
audit.levelReason: A supplied concrete definition supports a B1 polysemy decision.
audit.similarityNote: Meaning of term, not a second definition-identification task.

items.setupText: The diagram shows how paper is made, from preparing the fibers to drying the sheets.
items.taskText: What does 'process' refer to in 'the paper-making process'?
options: the quality rating of the finished paper
the tools listed beside the diagram
the person who drew the diagram
the connected stages of making paper
items.answer: the connected stages of making paper
items.explanation: A process is a series of actions or changes leading toward a result.

rationales.the connected stages of making paper: A process is a series of actions or changes leading toward a result.
rationales.the quality rating of the finished paper: A rating evaluates the result rather than describes how it is produced.
rationales.the tools listed beside the diagram: Tools are used during the process but are not the sequence of actions.
rationales.the person who drew the diagram: The designer is not the production process shown.

findings: Two-week process named only a duration and offered mostly nonnoun alternatives.
audit.microSkill: Process as connected stages
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates a sequence of production from tools, product quality and authorship.
audit.levelReason: A concrete manufacturing sequence makes an abstract B1 noun accessible.
audit.similarityNote: Production stages, not a prescribed workplace procedure.

items.setupText: A tutor likes an essay's ideas but suggests moving the explanation before the examples to improve its structure.
items.taskText: What is the tutor asking the writer to change?
options: the spelling of individual words
the subject being discussed
the size of the printed letters
the way the parts are arranged
items.answer: the way the parts are arranged
items.explanation: 'Structure' is the organization of a text; moving explanation and examples changes that organization.

rationales.the spelling of individual words: Spelling concerns word forms; the suggestion changes the order of parts.
rationales.the way the parts are arranged: 'Structure' is the organization of a text; moving explanation and examples changes that organization.
rationales.the subject being discussed: The tutor keeps the ideas and changes their arrangement, not the topic.
rationales.the size of the printed letters: Print size concerns appearance rather than the order of the reasoning.

findings: Clear-structure sentence gave no organizational feature to evaluate.
audit.microSkill: Structure as arrangement rather than content or typography
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects editorial feedback to a specific organizational revision.
audit.levelReason: An explanation-and-example sequence supports B1 writing vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Reordering content, not identifying a report section.

items.setupText: A questionnaire was sent to 80 learners. Forty respondents returned completed forms.
items.taskText: Who are the respondents?
options: the people who answered the questionnaire
the people who designed the questions
all the people who received a form
the people who checked the completed forms
items.answer: the people who answered the questionnaire
items.explanation: A respondent is someone who responds to questions, especially in a survey.

rationales.the people who designed the questions: Designers create the questionnaire; respondents supply answers.
rationales.all the people who received a form: Receiving a form does not make someone a respondent if no response is given.
rationales.the people who answered the questionnair: A respondent is someone who responds to questions, especially in a survey.
rationales.the people who checked the completed for: Checking responses is a separate role from providing them.

findings: Participants responded online used an irrelevant notice-board wrapper and did not distinguish study roles.
audit.microSkill: Respondent versus recipient or researcher
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates answering a questionnaire from being invited or analyzing answers.
audit.levelReason: Simple invitation and response counts support B1 role vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Participant role, not A2's survey-purpose distinction.

items.setupText: The project leader selected five photographs because each showed a different stage of construction.
items.taskText: Which statement preserves what 'selected' means here?
options: She took five new photographs.
She approved every photograph submitted.
She arranged the photographs by date.
She chose five photographs for the project.
items.answer: She chose five photographs for the project.
items.explanation: 'Select' means choose from available possibilities; the context gives a reason for the choice.

Selecting chooses among photographs; it does not say she created them.
Selecting five is not approving the whole collection.
Selection chooses the images; their ordering is a separate step.
rationales.She chose five photographs for the proje: 'Select' means choose from available possibilities; the context gives a reason for the choice.

findings: Select mapped to choose against three noun definitions, making the key easy by form alone.
audit.microSkill: Select versus create, approve and arrange
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes choosing material from other editorial operations.
audit.levelReason: A practical project choice with a stated criterion suits B1.
audit.similarityNote: Selection action, not random sampling or source evaluation.

items.setupText: Attendance was 60, 65, 63, 70 and 74 over five weeks. The report describes an upward trend.
items.taskText: What does 'upward trend' mean?
options: an increase in every single week
an overall movement toward higher numbers
the highest number on one particular day
the target set before the course began
items.answer: an overall movement toward higher numbers
items.explanation: A trend is a general direction; a small fall can occur within an overall rise.

rationales.an overall movement toward higher number: A trend is a general direction; a small fall can occur within an overall rise.
rationales.an increase in every single week: There was a fall from 65 to 63; a trend need not be uninterrupted.
rationales.the highest number on one particular day: A trend concerns a pattern across time, not one maximum.
rationales.the target set before the course began: These are observed attendance figures, not an intended target.

findings: Trend continued for months supplied no series and did not teach the difference between general and uninterrupted change.
audit.microSkill: Trend as general direction despite fluctuation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids interpreting an upward trend as a rise at every step.
audit.levelReason: A short, easily compared number series supports B1.
audit.similarityNote: Pattern across time, not mean, total or forecast.

items.setupText: The last page of the essay lists the authors, titles and publication dates of the works used.
items.taskText: What is this reference list mainly for?
options: to help readers identify the works used
to show which books the writer plans to buy
to repeat every sentence from those works
to give the writer's weekly study schedule
items.answer: to help readers identify the works used
items.explanation: A reference list gives details that identify the sources behind the writing.

rationales.to show which books the writer plans to: The list records works used in the essay, not future purchases.
rationales.to help readers identify the works used: A reference list gives details that identify the sources behind the writing.
rationales.to repeat every sentence from those work: References identify sources; they do not reproduce their full contents.
rationales.to give the writer's weekly study schedu: Publication details are not the writer's study times.

findings: Source is listed below repeated the A2 source definition without added demand.
audit.microSkill: Reference list as source identification
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains the purpose of bibliographic details without assuming a citation style.
audit.levelReason: Familiar author/title/date fields extend source literacy at B1.
audit.similarityNote: Identifying works in a list, not locating the original source in a story.

items.setupText: A study of town travel asked only people at a cycle club. The tutor warns of bias in the sample.
items.taskText: What is the concern?
options: Cyclists' experiences may be overrepresented.
The answers must have been invented.
The club members could not understand the questions.
The survey must contain too many questions.
items.answer: Cyclists' experiences may be overrepresented.
items.explanation: 'Bias' here is an uneven selection that may distort the picture of the wider town.

A biased sample can contain honest answers; fabrication is a different problem.
rationales.The club members could not understand th: No comprehension problem is described; the concern is who was included.
rationales.Cyclists' experiences may be overreprese: 'Bias' here is an uneven selection that may distort the picture of the wider town.
rationales.The survey must contain too many questio: The number of questions is not the sampling issue described.

findings: Unfair influence on judgment moralized sampling bias and did not describe any sampling problem.
audit.microSkill: Sample bias without assuming dishonesty
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes uneven representation from invented answers or confusing questions.
audit.levelReason: A familiar club and wider town provide a concrete B1 foundation.
audit.similarityNote: Who is included, not advanced statistical adjustment or personal prejudice.

items.setupText: Lena explains an author's idea in her own words and gives the author's name and the book details.
items.taskText: She cites the book but does not quote it. What is the distinction?
options: 'Citing' means agreeing with the author.
'Quoting' means changing the author's wording.
'Citing' names a source; 'quoting' reproduces its wording.
'Citing' means naming a source without using its ideas.
items.answer: 'Citing' names a source; 'quoting' reproduces its wording.
items.explanation: A citation points to a source, while a quotation reproduces wording from it.

A writer can cite a source while disagreeing with it.
rationales.'Quoting' means changing the author's wo: Quoting reproduces the original words rather than replaces them.
rationales.'Citing' means naming a source without u: A citation can acknowledge ideas used in the text, as Lena's does here.
rationales.'Citing' names a source; 'quoting' repro: A citation points to a source, while a quotation reproduces wording from it.

findings: Mention as evidence was too narrow: citations can identify material discussed or criticized, not only support.
audit.microSkill: Cite versus quote
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates source acknowledgment from exact reproduction and endorsement.
audit.levelReason: A concrete own-words account supports B1 source-use vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Citation action, not the purpose of the whole reference list.

items.setupText: The sentence says, 'After rowing all morning, we stopped at the bank for lunch.'
items.taskText: A tutor says to use the context to understand 'bank'. What should the learner use?
options: the surrounding words about the activity
the number of letters in 'bank'
the first meaning in any dictionary entry
the typeface used to print bank
items.answer: the surrounding words about the activity
items.explanation: Context includes nearby language and the situation; rowing helps suggest a river bank here.

rationales.the surrounding words about the activity: Context includes nearby language and the situation; rowing helps suggest a river bank here.
rationales.the number of letters in 'bank': Word length does not distinguish the place beside a river from a financial bank.
rationales.the first meaning in any dictionary entr: Dictionary order alone does not show which meaning fits this sentence.
rationales.the typeface used to print bank: Typeface does not explain the sense suggested by the activity.

findings: Context changes meaning was an unsupported generality without surrounding language to examine.
audit.microSkill: Context as surrounding language and situation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how contextual clues guide a sense choice without treating the clue as proof of necessity.
audit.levelReason: A familiar ambiguous noun and a short activity context suit B1.
audit.similarityNote: Using context to interpret a word, not selecting a register for an audience.

items.setupText: Before measuring anything, the team proposes that shaded rooms stay cooler than otherwise similar rooms in direct sun. It plans a comparison.
items.taskText: Why is the proposal a hypothesis in this study?
options: It is the full list of measurements already collected.
It is a conclusion that no longer needs testing.
It is a proposed relationship that can be tested.
It is the procedure for installing the thermometers.
items.answer: It is a proposed relationship that can be tested.
items.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable proposal or explanation; the room comparison can provide evidence about it.

rationales.It is the full list of measurements alre: Measurements would be data; the proposal comes before collection.
rationales.It is a conclusion that no longer needs: A hypothesis is proposed for investigation, not exempted from testing.
rationales.It is a proposed relationship that can b: A hypothesis is a testable proposal or explanation; the room comparison can provide evidence about it.
rationales.It is the procedure for installing the t: A procedure specifies actions; this proposal states an expected relationship.

findings: Experiment tested a hypothesis simply repeated the definition and supplied no proposed relationship.
audit.microSkill: Hypothesis versus data, conclusion and procedure
audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies the role of a testable proposal in an investigation.
audit.levelReason: A controlled comparison with a proposed relationship suits B2.
audit.similarityNote: Research proposal status, not a mere unverified planning assumption.

items.setupText: A reading study records each participant's age and usual reading time without asking anyone to change either.
items.taskText: Why can both be called variables?
options: Their values can differ among participants.
The researchers deliberately changed both.
Both are errors in the study design.
They are the study's written instructions.
items.answer: Their values can differ among participants.
items.explanation: A variable can vary across people or observations, even when the researcher does not manipulate it.

rationales.The researchers deliberately changed bot: Variables can be observed; manipulation is not required.
A variable is a characteristic that can take different values, not necessarily a flaw.
rationales.They are the study's written instruction: Instructions tell participants what to do; age and reading time are recorded characteristics.
rationales.Their values can differ among participan: A variable can vary across people or observations, even when the researcher does not manipulate it.

findings: Something that can change was underspecified and the clinic tail added no distinction between observation and manipulation.
audit.microSkill: Observed variable versus manipulated factor
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents the misconception that every research variable must be changed by an experimenter.
audit.levelReason: Two measured characteristics support a B2 methodological distinction.
audit.similarityNote: Variation in recorded attributes, not scope of a report.

items.setupText: An assignment asks you to paraphrase a short passage while keeping its full meaning, not reducing it to its main point.
items.taskText: Which action fulfills that instruction?
options: Reproduce the passage inside quotation marks.
Keep only the central idea and omit the rest.
Correct the writer's argument with your own evidence.
Express the passage's ideas in new wording.
items.answer: Express the passage's ideas in new wording.
items.explanation: Paraphrasing restates meaning in different wording; it is not necessarily a shorter summary.

rationales.Express the passage's ideas in new wordi: Paraphrasing restates meaning in different wording; it is not necessarily a shorter summary.
rationales.Reproduce the passage inside quotation m: That is quotation, which preserves the original wording.
